source_text: MEDEA. Women of Corinth, I am come to show My face, lest ye despise me. For I know Some heads stand high and fail not, even at night Alone--far less like this, in all men's sight: And we, who study not our wayfarings But feel and cry--Oh we are drifting things, And evil! For what truth is in men's eyes, Which search no heart, but in a flash despise A strange face, shuddering back from one that ne'er Hath wronged them? . . . Sure, far-comers anywhere, I know, must bow them and be gentle. Nay, A Greek himself men praise not, who alway Should seek his own will recking not. . . . But I-- This thing undreamed of, sudden from on high, Hath sapped my soul: I dazzle where I stand, The cup of all life shattered in my hand, Longing to die--O friends! He, even he, Whom to know well was all the world to me, The man I loved, hath proved most evil.--Oh, Of all things upon earth that bleed and grow, A herb most bruised is woman. We must pay Our store of gold, hoarded for that one day, To buy us some man's love; and lo, they bring A master of our flesh! There comes the sting Of the whole shame. And then the jeopardy, For good or ill, what shall that master be; Reject she cannot: and if he but stays His suit, 'tis shame on all that woman's days. So thrown amid new laws, new places, why, 'Tis magic she must have, or prophecy-- Home never taught her that--how best to guide Toward peace this thing that sleepeth at her side. And she who, labouring long, shall find some way Whereby her lord may bear with her, nor fray His yoke too fiercely, blessed is the breath That woman draws! Else, let her pray for death. Her lord, if he be wearied of the face Withindoors, gets him forth; some merrier place Will ease his heart: but she waits on, her whole Vision enchained on a single soul. And then, forsooth, 'tis they that face the call Of war, while we sit sheltered, hid from all Peril!--False mocking! Sooner would I stand Three times to face their battles, shield in hand, Than bear one child. But peace! There cannot be Ever the same tale told of thee and me. Thou hast this city, and thy father's home, And joy of friends, and hope in days to come: But I, being citiless, am cast aside By him that wedded me, a savage bride Won in far seas and left--no mother near, No brother, not one kinsman anywhere For harbour in this storm. Therefore of thee I ask one thing. If chance yet ope to me Some path, if even now my hand can win Strength to requite this Jason for his sin, Betray me not! Oh, in all things but this, I know how full of fears a woman is, And faint at need, and shrinking from the light Of battle: but once spoil her of her right In man's love, and there moves, I warn thee well, No bloodier spirit between heaven and hell.
modern_text: MEDEA. Women of Corinth, I have come out so you can see my face — I would not have you despise me. I know that some heads stand high and never falter, even at night, alone — let alone in plain sight of men. And the rest of us, who do not measure each step but feel and cry out — oh, we are drifting, evil things. For what truth is there in men's eyes, that search no heart but in a flash despise a strange face, recoiling from someone who has never wronged them? I know — strangers anywhere must bow themselves and be gentle. Even a Greek wins no praise if he always pursues his own will without regard for others. But this thing — this unimagined blow falling on me out of the sky — has emptied my soul. I dazzle where I stand, the cup of all my life shattered in my hand, longing to die. O my friends — he, the very man whom to know well was the whole world to me, the man I loved — has shown himself most evil. Of all things on earth that bleed and grow, woman is the most bruised herb. We must pay our hoard of gold, saved up for that one day, to buy ourselves a man's love — and what they bring us is a master of our flesh. There begins the whole shame. Then the gamble — for good or ill — what kind of master will he be? She cannot refuse him; and if he so much as hesitates in his courtship, every day of her life is shamed. Thrown into new laws, a new home — she would need magic, or prophecy (no one taught her these things at home) to know how best to manage this thing that sleeps at her side. And the woman who, after long labor, finds some way to make her husband bear with her without straining the yoke too fiercely — blessed is the breath that woman draws. Otherwise, let her pray for death. Her lord, if he gets bored of the face inside the house, goes out — some merrier place will ease his heart. But she waits, her whole vision chained to a single soul. And then, forsooth, they tell us they are the ones who face the call of war while we sit sheltered, hidden from all peril. False mockery. I would rather stand three times to face their battles, shield in hand, than bear one child. But peace — your story and mine cannot be the same. You have this city, your father's home, the joy of friends, hope for the days to come. But I, with no city, am cast aside by the man who married me, a foreign bride won in distant seas and abandoned — no mother near me, no brother, no kin anywhere to take me in out of this storm. So I ask one thing of you. If chance opens some path for me, if my hand can yet find strength to pay Jason back for his sin — do not betray me. In all things else, I know how full of fears a woman is, how faint at need, how she shrinks from the light of battle. But once rob her of her right in a man's love, and there is no bloodier spirit between heaven and hell — I warn you well.

source_text: NURSE. Would God no Argo e'er had winged the seas To Colchis through the blue Symplegades: No shaft of riven pine in Pelion's glen Shaped that first oar-blade in the hands of men Valiant, who won, to save King Pelias' vow, The fleece All-golden! Never then, I trow, Mine own princess, her spirit wounded sore With love of Jason, to the encastled shore Had sailed of old Iolcos: never wrought The daughters of King Pelias, knowing not, To spill their father's life: nor fled in fear, Hunted for that fierce sin, to Corinth here With Jason and her babes. This folk at need Stood friend to her, and she in word and deed Served alway Jason. Surely this doth bind, Through all ill days, the hurts of humankind, When man and woman in one music move. But now, the world is angry, and true love Sick as with poison. Jason doth forsake My mistress and his own two sons, to make His couch in a king's chamber. He must wed: Wed with this Creon's child, who now is head And chief of Corinth. Wherefore sore betrayed Medea calleth up the oath they made, They two, and wakes the clasped hands again, The troth surpassing speech, and cries amain On God in heaven to mark the end, and how Jason hath paid his debt. All fasting now And cold, her body yielded up to pain, Her days a waste of weeping, she hath lain, Since first she knew that he was false. Her eyes Are lifted not; and all her visage lies In the dust. If friends will speak, she hears no more Than some dead rock or wave that beats the shore: Only the white throat in a sudden shame May writhe, and all alone she moans the name Of father, and land, and home, forsook that day For this man's sake, who casteth her away. Not to be quite shut out from home . . . alas, She knoweth now how rare a thing that was! Methinks she hath a dread, not joy, to see Her children near. 'Tis this that maketh me Most tremble, lest she do I know not what. Her heart is no light thing, and useth not To brook much wrong. I know that woman, aye, And dread her! Will she creep alone to die Bleeding in that old room, where still is laid Lord Jason's bed? She hath for that a blade Made keen. Or slay the bridegroom and the king, And win herself God knows what direr thing? 'Tis a fell spirit. Few, I ween, shall stir Her hate unscathed, or lightly humble her. Ha! 'Tis the children from their games again, Rested and gay; and all their mother's pain Forgotten! Young lives ever turn from gloom!
modern_text: NURSE. If only the Argo had never spread its wings across the sea to Colchis through the dark Symplegades. If only no pine had ever been split in the glens of Pelion to shape that first oar in the hands of brave men, who sailed to win the All-Golden Fleece for King Pelias. Then my own princess, Medea, her heart torn open by love for Jason, would never have sailed to the towered shores of old Iolcus. The daughters of King Pelias, deceived, would never have spilled their father's blood. She would never have fled in terror, hunted for that fierce sin, here to Corinth with Jason and her children. The people of this country welcomed her in her need, and she, in word and deed, served Jason faithfully. Surely this is what holds humanity together through every dark day — when husband and wife move in one music. But now the world is bitter, and true love sickens like a poisoned thing. Jason has abandoned my mistress and his own two sons to make his bed in a king's chamber. He is taking a new wife: Creon's daughter, who now is head and chief of Corinth. Betrayed to the bone, Medea cries out the oath the two of them swore, calls back the clasped hands, the pledge that words cannot describe, and begs God in heaven to witness the end — to see how Jason has paid his debt. She has been fasting, cold, her body given over to pain, her days wasted in weeping, ever since she learned he was false. Her eyes never lift; her face stays in the dust. If friends try to speak to her, she hears no more than a dead rock or a wave breaking on the shore. Only the white throat sometimes writhes in sudden shame, and alone she moans the names of her father, her country, her home — all of it abandoned for the sake of this man who is throwing her away. Now, locked out from any home — alas, she knows now how rare a thing that was. I think she dreads, rather than welcomes, the sight of her children near her. That is what makes me tremble most: that she may do — I don't know what. Her heart is no light thing; it does not bear injury well. I know that woman, yes, and I am afraid of her. Will she creep alone into that old room where Jason's bed still lies, and bleed to death? She has a sharpened blade for it. Or will she kill the bridegroom and the king, and bring some worse thing on herself? She is a fierce spirit. Few, I think, will rouse her hatred and walk away unhurt; she is not easily humbled. Ah! Here come the children back from their games, rested and happy, with no thought of their mother's pain. Young lives always turn away from gloom.

source_text: MEDEA. I will endure.--Go thou within, and lay All ready that my sons may need to-day. O children, children mine: and you have found A land and home, where, leaving me discrowned And desolate, forever you will stay, Motherless children! And I go my way To other lands, an exile, ere you bring Your fruits home, ere I see you prospering Or know your brides, or deck the bridal bed, All flowers, and lift your torches overhead. Oh cursed be mine own hard heart! 'Twas all In vain, then, that I reared you up, so tall And fair; in vain I bore you, and was torn With those long pitiless pains, when you were born. Ah, wondrous hopes my poor heart had in you, How you would tend me in mine age, and do The shroud about me with your own dear hands, When I lay cold, blessed in all the lands That knew us. And that gentle thought is dead! You go, and I live on, to eat the bread Of long years, to myself most full of pain. And never your dear eyes, never again, Shall see your mother, far away being thrown To other shapes of life. . . . My babes, my own, Why gaze ye so?--What is it that ye see?-- And laugh with that last laughter? . . . Woe is me, What shall I do? Women, my strength is gone, Gone like a dream, since once I looked upon Those shining faces. . . . I can do it not. Good-bye to all the thoughts that burned so hot Aforetime! I will take and hide them far, Far, from men's eyes. Why should I seek a war So blind: by these babes' wounds to sting again Their father's heart, and win myself a pain Twice deeper? Never, never! I forget Henceforward all I laboured for. And yet, What is it with me? Would I be a thing Mocked at, and leave mine enemies to sting Unsmitten? It must be. O coward heart, Ever to harbour such soft words!--Depart Out of my sight, ye twain.      [_The_ CHILDREN _go in_. And they whose eyes Shall hold it sin to share my sacrifice, On their heads be it! My hand shall swerve not now. Ah, Ah, thou Wrath within me! Do not thou, Do not. . . . Down, down, thou tortured thing, and spare My children! They will dwell with us, aye, there Far off, and give thee peace. Too late, too late! By all Hell's living agonies of hate, They shall not take my little ones alive To make their mock with! Howsoe'er I strive The thing is doomed; it shall not escape now From being. Aye, the crown is on the brow, And the robe girt, and in the robe that high Queen dying. I know all. Yet . . . seeing that I Must go so long a journey, and these twain A longer yet and darker, I would fain Speak with them, ere I go. Come, children; stand A little from me. There. Reach out your hand, Your right hand--so--to mother: and good-bye! Oh, darling hand! Oh, darling mouth, and eye, And royal mien, and bright brave faces clear, May you be blessed, but not here! What here Was yours, your father stole. . . . Ah God, the glow Of cheek on cheek, the tender touch; and Oh, Sweet scent of childhood. . . . Go! Go! . . . Am I blind? . . . Mine eyes can see not, when I look to find Their places. I am broken by the wings Of evil. . . . Yea, I know to what bad things I go, but louder than all thought doth cry Anger, which maketh man's worst misery. [MEDEA _comes out alone from the house_.
modern_text: MEDEA. I will endure. — Go inside, and lay everything ready that my sons will need today. O children, children of mine — you have found a land and a home, where you will stay forever, leaving me uncrowned and desolate — motherless children. And I go my way to other lands, an exile, before you bring your fruits home, before I see you prospering, before I know your brides or deck the bridal bed with flowers, or hold your torches overhead. Oh, cursed be my own hard heart. It was all in vain, then, that I raised you up so tall and fair — in vain I carried you and was torn with those long, merciless pains when you were born. Ah, the wonderful hopes my poor heart had for you — how you would tend me in my old age, and lay the shroud about me with your own dear hands, when I lay cold, blessed in every land that knew us. And that gentle thought is dead. You go, and I live on, to eat the bread of long years, my own pain unending. Never again will those dear eyes see their mother, far away, thrown into other shapes of life. My babies — my own — why do you look at me like that? What is it you see? And why laugh with that last laughter? Woe is me, what shall I do? Women — my strength is gone, gone like a dream, since I looked at those shining faces. I cannot do it. Good-bye to all the thoughts that burned so hot before. I will take them and hide them far, far from men's eyes. Why should I wage so blind a war — to sting their father's heart through these babies' wounds and win myself a pain twice as deep? Never, never. From now on I forget all I worked for. And yet — what is happening to me? Will I be a thing to be mocked, and leave my enemies to sting on, unsmitten? It must be. O coward heart, ever to harbor such soft words. Get out of my sight, you two. [The CHILDREN go in.] And those whose eyes will count it sin to share my sacrifice — let it be on their heads. My hand will not swerve now. Ah, ah — Wrath within me — do not — do not. Down, down, you tortured thing, and spare my children. They will live with us, far off, and give you peace. Too late, too late. By all Hell's living agonies of hate, they shall not take my little ones alive to make a mockery. However I struggle, the thing is doomed; it cannot escape now from being done. Yes — the crown is on her brow, the robe is wrapped about her, and in that robe the high Queen is dying. I know it all. Yet — since I must go on so long a journey, and these two on a longer and darker one — I would speak with them once before I go. Come, children — stand a little away from me. There. Reach out your hand — your right hand — so — to mother. Good-bye. Oh, darling hand. Oh, darling mouth, darling eye, and royal bearing, and bright brave clear faces — may you be blessed, but not here. Whatever was yours here, your father stole. Ah, God — the glow of cheek on cheek, the tender touch — and oh, the sweet scent of childhood. Go. Go. Am I blind? My eyes can see nothing when I look to find their places. I am broken by the wings of evil. Yes, I know what bad things I am going to. But louder than all thought, Anger cries — Anger, which makes man's worst misery. [MEDEA comes out alone from the house.]
